The Grandeur was the first to launch with Hyundai’s Pleos in Korea in May, followed by the IONIQ 3 in Europe. In the US, the fresh Tucson will be the first to go on sale with Pleos in early 2027.

Recent findings suggest that is the IONIQ 5 next in line? Hyundai aims to launch its first SDV as early as next year, and the IONIQ 5 appears to be a contender.

An IONIQ 5 test car was captured again (shown below) by @JHS_spyshot_official in a Korean parking garage, but this time the door was wide open, offering a clear view of the fresh setup.

A post shared by JHS (@jhs_spyshot_official).

Hyundai appeared to be testing automated parking features, and as you can see, the setup is considerably different from the current IONIQ 5.

Sources indicate that A large infotainment display sits at the center that appears to be running Hyundai Pleos, instead of the current dual 12.3″ screens. Meanwhile, the steering wheel and dash both appear to be completely redesigned.

Although it’s hard to see, previous spy images show the IONIQ 5 SDV test car with no driver display, with all information expected to move to the large center infotainment screen.

By 2030, Hyundai Motor Group plans to equip around 20 million Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis vehicles with the newly introduced Pleos setup.

Guess I'm holding onto my 2023 EV6 for as long as I can. I saw a preview of the new software and think it looks pretty solid, but I am NOT a fan of the "huge tablet" dashboard.

My dad has a newly introduced Solterra and we took a long road trip in my EV6 last month. He said my screens are so much more easy to see and use. The only issue I have is the top of the steering wheel obscures the icons at the top of my driver's screen, but I'd rather have that than a giant hulking tablet sitting in the middle of the dash.

The system is the “first tangible step” toward an SDV (Software-Defined Vehicle) architecture, Hyundai said, which will unlock new in-car features, autonomous driving capabilities, and personalized driving experiences.

Over the summer, an IONIQ 6 prototype was spotted near Hyundai’s R&D hub in Europe with a similar high-tech setup.

With Hyundai planning to launch its first SDV as early as next year, we should learn more soon.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 02:00 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Industry observers note that formal verification startup Sequent Inc. today confirmed that it has raised $2.2 million in fresh funding to take its Alan proof platform out of early access.

According to recent reports, founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set. Decentralized exchange Curve Finance is its first paying customer.

Curve also figures in how Sequent got started. Chief Executive Charles Cooper, who leads development of Vyper, one of the two main programming languages for Ethereum, inadvertently introduced a flaw into the Vyper compiler in 2021. Though the bug was fixed within months, programs already running on the blockchain could not be updated, leaving older Curve pools and other projects exposed when attackers used the flaw to take more than $50 million in July 2023.

Following the incident, Ramana Kumar, now Sequent’s chief technology officer and formerly an AI safety researcher at Google DeepMind, offered to help prove the Vyper compiler correct. Kumar co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct all the way down to the instructions a computer runs.

Cooper believes the lesson reaches far beyond crypto, saying that “smart contracts taught us that anything that can be exploited will be.” Banks, governments and companies running older systems have relied on keeping their code private, according to Cooper, who noted AI-powered cyberattacks are now eroding that protection.

Alan works today on Vyper smart contracts, with support for Solidity and Solana in development and general software in Rust, C, TypeScript and Python to follow.

Recent findings suggest that for now, engineers using Alan write rules for their code such as “no user can withdraw more than their balance” in plain language, and the job of finding a mathematical proof is handed to AI. Nothing the AI comes up with is taken on trust, as each proof has to get through HOL4, a checker Kumar has helped build for more than a decade.

In a recent development, for two-coin StableSwap pools holding standard tokens, Alan was used to prove that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order. The work also found minor accounting and rounding errors, none of which breached the limit. The founders are now proving the Vyper compiler itself, since the Curve proof does not cover the compiler where the 2021 flaw sat.

Sources indicate that along with AI computing costs, the funding will pay for engineering, sales and marketing hires. Subscriptions to Alan start at $99 a month for individuals, with auditor plans priced at $200 a month and team plans starting at $500 a month.

Sources indicate that frachtis and Metaplanet Holdings OÜ co-led the pre-seed round. Metaplanet is the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic PBC’s Series A round in 2021. According to Frachtis founder Xavier Meegan, crypto is the right place to start, with “billions already at risk.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving week has been crazy so far, with a stock rally, stocks selling off, the 10-year yield dropping below 4.85%, tariffs being announced, inflation running hot, low jobless claims, strong GDP data and then — the housing data surprised to the upside! Let’s look at what’s happening as mortgage rates have fallen a tad from recent highs.

It has been revealed that as we’ve discussed in the Housing Market Tracker articles over the past few weeks, our weekly pending sales data has stabilized and last week it grew a bit. The housing market took a shock when rates rose aggressively from under 7% in September to 7.61% in early October; that shock really impacted demand, but rates haven’t gone higher than that and have eased a bit since.

Those lower rates stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, which grew last week.

Recent findings suggest that purchase application data, on the other hand, has moved more noticeably. This index can be very tricky at times because it’s a survey, but to see this growth without rates below 7% is a good sign of stabilization.

Of course, the year-over-year purchase application data is still down big, but last year mortgage rates were roughly 1% lower at this time and we were heading toward a nine-month high in sales last December.

Newly introduced home sales today beat estimates so much that my first inclination was not to believe it! I expect this number will be revised lower, but it’s still a positive trend. New home sales are basically doing the same thing they have done for 10 years, outside the COVID sales burst. They don’t really go below 570,000, nor do they really break away from 730,000. We are stuck in this range, as the builders are still working in a sub-6 % mortgage market, and thus new home sales are still at 2019 levels. If existing home sales were operating at those levels it would amount to 1-1.3 million more existing home sales. However, the existing home market hasn’t had the luxury of sub-6 % mortgage rates.

One positive note that isn’t getting a lot of play is that the builders are slowly moving their completed units of sale lower. If we want housing starts to ever grow again, this needs to happen and fortunately this number has been falling all year long.

As I am writing this article, the 10-year yield is at 4.82%.

If we want sub-7 % rates for Thanksgiving, Christmas, or Latest Year’s — as I have written about for weeks — we need the 10-year yield at 4.85% and under. Now, if spreads just improve a little, then we get our sub-7 % mortgage rates for the holidays. It’s been a wild week, folks; enjoy the holiday!

Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson responded to frustrated Cardano community members who are disappointed by the blockchain’s pace of development and inability to rebound from the current slump.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 21, Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson took to X to counter criticism about the current state of Cardano.

The exchange was triggered by a joke made by an X user stating that Grand Theft Auto 6 came out before a working Cardano blockchain.

Hoskinson replied to the comment, saying: “Cardano works.”.

Later, Hoskinson addressed the poor price performance of the cryptocurrency and explained that price doesn’t always reflect the capabilities of blockchain networks.

Sources indicate that “Yeah. Price doesn't equal utility. Is Solana 75 percent less capable than it's all time high? It's an infinitely better product today for many more people. And so it is for Cardano,” he stated.

What this means is that even if the value of a blockchain network's native cryptocurrency is dropping, the technology can still advance.

An X user, however, contested his comparison with Solana, stating that Cardano hasn’t been able to retake its previous all-time high even after years of development.

This drew an increasingly irritated response from Hoskinson.

Industry observers note that “So every single thing a f****** scam? Everything they do failed? I’m so tired of you people,” mentioned the Cardano founder.

This recent statement by Hoskinson comes as Cardano (ADA) remains one of the worst-performing major cryptocurrencies in the current market downturn.

As per CoinGlass data, ADA is right now trading at around $0.14. The cryptocurrency is down by about 57% since the beginning of 2026.

It has lost a whopping 95.4% of its value from its all-time high of $3.09, set in September 2021.

On Nov. 21, ADA briefly dipped toward $0.13. This came as another sell-off hit the broader crypto market.

Cardano has been in a steady decline, leading to criticism regarding its adoption, activity in its ecosystem and ability to compete with the likes of Ethereum and Solana.

Nonetheless, Charles Hoskinson has maintained that short-term market performance should not be conflated with the progress of blockchain technology over the long run.

Earlier this month, the Cardano founder tried to reassure frustrated ADA holders and tell them that things would eventually get better.

“It's all going to be ok. Everyone will be happy next year after all this madness, hate and idiocy,” stated Hoskinson in a previous X post.

#134515. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO states

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (804 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO states

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.
  • Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005.
  • Sources indicate that pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents mentioned.

Sources indicate that pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint mentioned he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”.

It has been revealed that white also allegedly remarked that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or blueprint.”.

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also mentioned the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”.

Visualized with the help of AI.

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears mentioned the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

According to recent reports, “John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”.

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”.

Sources indicate that “Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”.

#134514. Tech Report: Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3648 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.
  • That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality.
  • Industry observers note that these models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:59 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.

That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality. Open-weight models, AI models whose trained parameters, or “weights,” are publicly available for others to download, run, customize and fine-tune, are the overnight sensation in an industry already moving at light speed.

Industry observers note that these models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods. They also carry a variety of license types that may restrict how they can be used commercially. But they offer choice, flexibility and cost advantages that the leading-edge “frontier” models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude don’t. For information technology organizations, they can be a respite from spiraling token costs.

The popularity of these models has soared as AI has matured and organizations have realized that not every use case demands the biggest and best solution. They come in various shapes and sizes, ranging from less than 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion parameters. Many are tuned for specific tasks, such as recognizing images or writing software. That gives organizations the flexibility to match the model to the job.

“Frontier intelligence is priced for the hardest problems, and most agent work isn’t hard,” said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of Anything, the business name of Create Inc. and developer of an AI-powered platform for building mobile and web applications. “Companies are chartering a jet to cross the street.”.

“There are lots of tasks in customer self-service and employee self-service that need a smaller model,” said Dheeraj Pandey, chief executive officer of DevRev Inc., maker of a unified customer support, software development and engineering platform.

DevRev created an open, vendor-neutral benchmark to measure how reliably enterprise AI agents perform in realistic organizational environments. “We get almost the same accuracy and precision on enterprise tasks, whether you use the open-weight models or the frontier models,” he mentioned.

According to recent reports, the ascendancy of open-weight models has been breathtaking. Vercel Inc.’s monthly AI Gateway report found that their share of observed token traffic surged from 7% last December to 56% in August and that the models held eight of the 10 busiest spots on OpenRouter Inc.’s large language model ranking in August by token volume.

Recent findings suggest that three-year-old OpenRouter itself turned heads in August when it sold to Stripe Inc. for an eye-popping $7.5 billion. The firm’s technology connects developers and customers with hundreds of AI models from dozens of providers through a single interface.

Sources indicate that in September, Nvidia Corp. paid nearly $13 billion for Hugging Face Inc., which hosts more than 3 million models. “For most enterprises, the practical path to an open-weight model — evaluate, fine-tune, quantize, deploy — runs through that hub,” wrote Zeus Kerravala, principal analyst at ZK Research, referring to Hugging Face.

Recent findings suggest that enterprises aren’t abandoning frontier models. Rather, they’re learning to fit the model to the problem. None of the experts SiliconANGLE contacted believes open-weight models are a threat to the massive players.

“All players can win because the market is growing and the number of places where it makes sense to deploy AI increases,” Amin said.

Recent findings suggest that cost is currently the principal driver of open-weight adoption. As AI use has evolved from question-and-response generative models to sophisticated multistep agentic workflows, inference costs have soared. Gartner Inc. predicts inference costs per agentic workflow will increase more than fivefold through 2028.

“They are quickly starting to rival even payroll expenses,” Amin stated.

By most accounts, frontier models still offer the greatest power and range of usage options. But the gap is closing. Mozilla’s September State of Open-Source AI report put the capability gap between leading open-weight models and proprietary frontier models at roughly four months, down from 18 months just two years ago.

“The differences in quality are starting to be outweighed by the differences in cost,” wrote Ioana Hreninciuc, co-founder of inference platform Runware Ltd. She noted that though proprietary models still lead on top-tier reasoning, “you probably don’t need a frontier model for 80% of what you do.”.

The pivot to open weights isn’t a zero-sum proposition. Low token prices can mask integration overhead, tool failures and operational risk. “Tokenomics,” or measuring, attributing and managing the cost of tokens, has become an essential information technology discipline.

Recent findings suggest that in a Hyper Labs Inc. survey conducted by The Harris Poll, 86% of AI leaders remarked managing token expenses is as critical as containing cloud costs. More than three-quarters said they are directing routine tasks to smaller models to protect budgets, while 89% have redesigned AI initiatives after getting token shock.

“The whole world is trying to solve for tokenomics,” said Armando Franco, senior director of cloud and platform modernization at IT services provider TEKsystems Inc.

Experts say open-weight models are well-suited for repetitive, routine workloads. “Basically, they work best when the task is clear and it’s easy enough to check if the work was done correctly,” remarked Louis Amira, CEO of Circuit & Chisel Inc., an AI infrastructure and agentic commerce startup.

Karen Panetta, an IEEE Fellow and dean of graduate education at Tufts University School of Engineering, said open models are flourishing as technology leaders learn to match the engine to the task.

According to recent reports, “If a bicycle will get you there, don’t pick the expensive sports car,” she mentioned. “You have to ask: What problem you are trying to solve?” She asserted that for applications that don’t require 99.9% precision, organizations can achieve massive savings with compact models.

Sources indicate that they’re also an attractive option when protecting customer data is a priority, since sensitive information never needs to leave the organization. “Customer data never, never goes into a frontier,” Scott Wallace, senior global director of solutions architecture at Digital Realty Inc., remarked in an interview with the Financial Times.

According to recent reports, sovereignty, or the ability to control and govern digital assets in line with local laws, security needs, and strategic interests, is a growing glitch for organizations. A Linux Foundation survey last year found that 79% of AI leaders — and 86% in the U.S. — rate sovereignty as a strategic priority.

“What began as a specialized concern for highly regulated industries is rapidly becoming a strategic consideration for nearly every enterprise,” Paul Nashawaty, a principal analyst at theCUBE Research, wrote in a recent analysis.

Some early adopters are demonstrating impressive returns.

Advocates point to a shrinking capability gap, too, with some open-weight models nipping at the heels of the frontier alternatives. Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co., Ltd.’s 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s 2.4 trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max nearly match closed models on coding benchmarks, according to Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute.

An agent built by Tenzai Inc. recently captured the top spot on HackerOne’s leaderboard using Z.ai Inc.’s GLM 5.2, generating 30% more findings per unit of computing power than a previous baseline using a proprietary model.

“What was the frontier 18 months ago is now well-mapped territory, and open-source models are closing the gap at a fraction of the cost” wrote Runware’s Hreninciuc.

Though such metrics explain open models’ ascendancy, the decision to use them isn’t open-and-shut. Experts cite four common myths that can mitigate the cost efficiencies.

Industry observers note that one is the mistaken belief that open-weight models conflate with traditional open-source software and its permissive licenses. “This is a misnomer among many enterprises,” said Dr. Dorotea Baljević, EMEA Lead for AI Advisory at technology research and advisory firm Information Services Group. “There is licensing for these models in most cases, particularly for commercial usage.”.

Although some, such as Qwen3, Mistral 3, Gemma 4 and DeepSeek V4, are covered by standard Apache or MIT licenses, terms and conditions vary. For example, Liquid AI Inc.’s open-weight models are free for commercial use only to organizations with less than $10 million in annual revenue.

“Other licenses require attribution, restrict certain application categories, or impose acceptable use policies, none of which carry a direct fee but all of which create legal exposure if ignored,” noted Bumu Technologies Inc., which does business as Nanobase.

Evaluating models for accuracy, stability and explainability also falls to the user. With thousands of open-weight models available, the costs of a bake-off between multiple candidates can add up.

Industry observers note that baljević suggests organizations consider whether the model will be used internally or externally, the organization’s tolerance for accuracy, strategic fit and switching costs as evaluation criteria. Performance on public benchmarks also doesn’t guarantee a model will work well with an organization’s data, workflows and language.

It has been revealed that finance leaders may look at the 80% to 90% cost advantage of open-weight tokens and assume operational expenditures will drop proportionally. But tokens are only one part of the cost equation and not necessarily even the biggest one.

Recent findings suggest that organizations that strategy to deploy models on their own infrastructure must bear the costs of integration, API development, IT infrastructure and human labor required for auditing and verification. A fraction of a cent saved on an inference call can be wiped out by the cost of a human expert spending a half-hour re-entering flawed database transactions.

In a recent development, lack of visibility into how the model is operating can also produce sticker shock. A retry loop, in which an agent tries repeatedly to complete a failed task, can go on for hours or even days. The Wall Street Journal recently reported on a case in which an AI-generated out-of-office message at a San Francisco-based software company went into a loop that ultimately burned $10,000 a day in token costs.

In a recent development, if a cheap open-weight model fails a multi-system query or generates invalid JSON, it triggers automated retries that can consume millions of secondary tokens. The human expertise required to repair the transaction manually can erase months of token savings.

“The core software engineering required to test and integrate latest models into the software stack is often the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities, APIs and such,” stated Alex Bakker, an ISG distinguished analyst. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”.

Using private graphics processing unit clusters eliminates external API fees, but self-hosting economics hinge on high, sustained utilization. Models that sit idle or at low usage levels consume power, create processing inefficiencies and incur costs if restarts are required.

Recent findings suggest that cast AI Group Inc. reported last spring that the average GPU utilization was 5% across thousands of clusters it monitored. Frontier models are usually a better option in that case. “Open models can be dramatically cheaper at high utilization, while frontier APIs remain cheaper for intermittent workloads because you aren’t paying for idle capacity,” said Arun Chandrasekaran, distinguished VP analyst at Gartner.

For intermittent workloads such as batch payroll processing or seasonal financial reporting, the organization pays 100% of capital expenses, power, cooling and depreciation while hardware idles.

“On-premises hosting wins when there is high, predictable 24/7 traffic where servers are constantly busy,” said Debojyoti Dutta, chief AI officer at Nutanix Inc. A hosted frontier model is a better choice “with spiky or lower traffic, where paying per token with zero setup cost is cheaper than renting idle hardware.”.

When AI agents fail, the default reaction is to switch to a newer model, but benchmark data demonstrates that approach is usually a dead end.

It has been revealed that most evaluation tests give agents relatively simple tasks and judge them mainly on whether they get the right answer. But real business environments are much more complicated. Agents must gather information from different systems, connect it correctly, handle growing amounts of data, and work within security rules.

This interface complexity is what usually breaks AI agents. DevRev estimates that moving an agent from clean test tools to real-world corporate use causes an 18% to 19% drop in accuracy. Upgrading the model improves performance by less than 1%.

According to recent reports, “Every time a newly introduced model comes out, you need to re-evaluate your benchmarks, your models and your fine-tuning processes,” mentioned Steven Yang, senior director of product management at Tanium Inc. That means better data integration is a more effective strategy than buying new models.

In a recent development, though the open-weight option is viable for any manufacturer, experts say the best use cases are those where control, accountability and performance are paramount. The following three factors are at least as important as cost.

Compliance: Regulated industries have been held back from adopting AI over data residency and confidentiality concerns. Deploying open weights within enterprise data centers or virtual private clouds reduces the need for external data egress, ensures zero training data retention and allows for total physical isolation. The models also allow inspection of internal mechanics such as log-probabilities, token confidence scores and loss landscapes.

Training datasets, model weights and inference prompts never cross borders or leave the organization’s physical perimeter. That makes it easier to comply with strict data localization laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act in the U.S. and the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe. Local auditing and observability also aid in compliance with regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act, which requires detailed logging, risk assessments and explainability.

But deploying on private infrastructure isn’t a cure-all. “You still have to maintain an aggressive data security posture around your processes because even open-weight models sometimes will take action trying to accomplish their tasks that could potentially violate some type of compliance rule,” noted TEKSystems’ Franco.

Transparency: Understanding how models arrive at an answer is critical in many scenarios, particularly those involving safety, law and finance. “Open-weight models expose the math behind their answers,” said Brian Weiss, chief technology officer at document processing platform maker Hyperscience, the business name of Hyper Labs Inc. “You can use that to hold the model accountable for accuracy.”.

In a recent development, in contrast, frontier APIs often obscure the equations used to generate probabilities, which are critical to assessing accuracy. Asking a model how confident it is in its answer may yield a subjective response. Open weights allow confidence scores to be scored against ground-truth outcomes for better reliability.

“People can take these models inside their organization, do some post-training and fine-tuning and have a customized model where they know the costs, where it’s sitting and what data is being sent to it,” said David DeSanto, CEO of Anaconda Inc., maker of an AI development platform.

“The future is an orchestrated ensemble of bounded, transparent, governed, cost-effective models,” Weiss noted. “If I find a better model for a particular task, I can swap it out because I have the framework to do that.”.

Performance: As organizations move from the relatively simple generative AI question-and-response metaphor to sophisticated multi-agent frameworks, latency problems can compound exponentially. For example, a 500-millisecond API delay across 50 sequential reasoning steps creates 25 seconds of cumulative latency, which would render many applications useless.

Recent findings suggest that executing open-weight models directly alongside operational databases or within containerized edge pods minimizes routing hops and rate limits. Distillation, which trains smaller, specialized open models from frontier “teacher” models, is faster.

Hyperscience reported that distillation delivers up to 97% cost reduction and four times faster inference, while retaining over 95% of the original model’s performance on designated tasks. Small models are faster and considerably cheaper than frontier LLMs.

Experts say constructing a business case for open-weight models requires understanding three major sources of hidden expense.

Complexity tax: Reasoning can break down when open-weight models interact with complex enterprise data at scale. The “Cartesian Shortcut” refers to a phenomenon in which AI models rely on workarounds learned during training rather than demonstrating a flexible understanding of the problem they’re trying to solve.

Recent findings suggest that google LLC researchers found that the models struggled with visual reasoning problems, such as solving mazes, when the data was presented in a circular rather than a grid layout. Leading models answered 69% to 83% of the square-grid problems correctly, but their accuracy fell to below 40% when the problems appeared in circular layouts.

Industry observers note that the corollary to a business scenario is a multihop join across multiple systems. Models may “cheat” by collapsing field-level relationships into hierarchical groupings, generating massive data fabrications.

Human oversight remains critical: “For validation and rework, humans in the loop need to be taken into account on top of all the tokens you’re paying for already,” stated TekSystems’ Franco.

Industry observers note that poor data quality: Foundation models can’t fix bad data, a fact that’s holding back AI adoption across the board. The Hyperscience/Harris Poll study found that 86% of IT leaders remarked dirty internal data is actively crippling GenAI performance.

Sources indicate that feeding error-strewn or outdated information into probabilistic models creates “context pollution,” the accumulation of irrelevant, redundant, outdated or contradictory information. When agents execute multistep database joins, system workflows or automated tool calls based on flawed data or ambiguous schemas, cascading errors can occur.

Sauce Labs Inc. Chief Technology Officer Anoop Tripathi recommends creating validated “golden datasets” for fine-tuning and evaluation. He also cautions architects against misapplying probabilistic AI to structured business logic. In other words, use models only where they add value and apply conventional (and cheaper) data processing to everything else.

In a recent development, continuous evaluation: Selecting the right model out of thousands of open-weight alternatives requires ongoing evaluation against internal workloads rather than public leaderboards. That demands expensive MLOps, site reliability engineering and platform engineering skills.

Because fresh models are constantly being introduced and revised, Circuit & Chisel’s Amira recommends building custom testing harnesses that can quickly evaluate candidate models against business-relevant tasks.

Sources indicate that rather than treating open-weight adoption as an all-or-nothing choice, enterprise architects should bucket organizational tasks into distinct operational tiers. Don’t feed every problem into a token-hungry trillion-parameter model if a smaller, specialized one will do the trick.

“Organizations don’t give a heavyweight reasoning model a lightweight sorting job,” said Nutanix’s Dutta. “They divide their business workloads into tiers based on cost, speed and hardware footprint.”.

Industry observers note that lower-tier workloads such as search, embeddings and document classification work well with inexpensive, compact open-weight and small language models. Sophisticated tasks such as autonomous reasoning and restructuring large, deeply entangled legacy software systems are better suited to commercial alternatives.

ISG’s Bakker believes the need for constant evaluation is the biggest impediment to open-weight adoption. “The core software engineering required to test and integrate upcoming models into the software stack will likely be the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities and APIs,” he said. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”.

Enterprise IT organizations must develop expertise in local model execution, containerized execution sandboxes and agent harness orchestration. Managing AI and agents safely “is, in the near future, going to be as vital an indigenous knowledge as how to upgrade Windows,” said Gordon Allott, founder and CEO of private infrastructure provider nFOX Lab.

The shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management. Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task. That’s a discipline that was barely on the roadmap a year ago.

According to recent reports, at the start of the year, there was no way enterprises were going to touch open-weight models, Brad Maltz, head of AI factory solutions at Dell Technologies Inc., stated in a November interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE’s streaming media platform. “People were pretty wrong about that. I think the open-weight movement is the future.”.

In a recent development, the token also lost 10% and 11.8% in November of 2021 and 2022, respectively. In November of 2023 and 2024, XRP gained 1.4% and 281.7%.

In a recent development, in November 2018, the crypto market crashed after the Bitcoin Cash hard fork, and XRP lost 19.3% that month. In December 2018, the token fell 2.25%. Two years earlier, XRP dropped 18% in November 2016 and 4.07% in December 2016.

Recent findings suggest that XRP's median December return is -4.07%, and its average December return is +63.1%, according to CryptoRank data. Most of that average comes from December 2017, when XRP gained 818.9%.

XRP has closed December in the red in eight of the past 13 years. In December of 2021, 2022 and 2025, the token lost 17%, 16.9% and 14.8%, respectively, and in December 2024, it gained 6.94%.

In a recent development, in 2020, XRP's December drop came as the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission sued Ripple on Dec. 22, 2020. The token lost 66.5% that month, and in January 2021, it gained 122.1%.

In 2025, XRP's December drop came after the token set its all-time high of $3.65 on July 18, 2025. XRP lost 13.8% in November 2025 and 14.8% in December, and in January 2026, it fell another 10.6%.

Industry observers note that so far in 2026, XRP has lost value in seven of 11 months. The token's biggest monthly drops this year came in June and November, when it lost 22.1% and 25.4%, respectively, according to CryptoRank. Its best month was August, with a 30% gain.

On Nov. 17, U.S. spot XRP ETFs had $1.08 billion in assets, according to SoSoValue. Since the start of November, the funds have lost about $26 million to outflows, and $19.13 million of that amount left in the week ending Nov. 13. Ripple's next monthly escrow release of 1 billion XRP is scheduled for Dec. 1.

Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse also commented on the sell-off on CNBC on Nov. 19. "What happens is you've got risk-on assets and people are taking liquidity out of a very liquid market, crypto included — Bitcoin, XRP — and moving it into SpaceX. The exact same thing happened coming into the Anthropic IPO. What we saw after the SpaceX IPO was a rally in the crypto markets. I think you'll see that happen here as well," he said.

XRP's November drop took the token to its lowest level in two years, according to TradingView data.

Tech Report: New home sales surge in October, but demand signals remain soft

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New home sales blipped above expectations in October, handing homebuilders a slice of better-than-worse, Thanksgiving-time, good news.
  • Census Bureau data, sales of newly constructed single-family homes in October came in at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 701,000, up 14.2% month-over month, and a 7.5% gain from the same month a year prior.
  • Recent findings suggest that october’s better-than-forecast results may surprise many, but they come with a catch: the survey’s margin of error and data collection cycle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New home sales blipped above expectations in October, handing homebuilders a slice of better-than-worse, Thanksgiving-time, good news. However, NAHB’s November homebuilder confidence gauge had plunged to its lowest level in nearly 15 years, signaling that builders remain pessimistic about the market’s current state and foreseeable-future direction.

According to U.S. Census Bureau data, sales of newly constructed single-family homes in October came in at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 701,000, up 14.2% month-over month, and a 7.5% gain from the same month a year prior. Meanwhile, the median sales price of fresh homes sold in October was $391,000, down 0.3% from September and 3.2% from a year ago.

Recent findings suggest that october’s better-than-forecast results may surprise many, but they come with a catch: the survey’s margin of error and data collection cycle. They could be revised downward next month.

“A downward revision to September helps explain the size of October’s 14.2% rebound, the largest monthly gain since November 2025,” First American Deputy Chief Economist Odeta Kushi said in a statement.

It has been revealed that new home for-sale inventory also tightened, coinciding with a decline in new residential construction. The seasonally adjusted estimate of new homes for sale at the end of October was 470,000, down 1.5% from September’s 477,000, and 4.1% below the 490,000 recorded in October 2025. At the current sales rate, that represents a supply of 8.0 months, a 14% improvement from 9.3 months in September and 11.1% from 9.0 months a year earlier.

October’s sales results may be less of a bright spot than they appear, and one strong month doesn’t erase the warning signs flashing across the upcoming home market.

Plenty of indications suggest homebuilders are working through one of the toughest housing markets in years, including homebuilder confidence at its lowest point since the tail end of the Great Financial Crisis.

According to recent reports, for example, mortgage applications for upcoming-home purchases fell 13.6% year over year in October, a sign that rising mortgage rates and low consumer confidence continue to weigh on demand. The existing-home market is also struggling, with the National Association of Realtors reporting that pending home sales fell to another record low in October.

NAHB also reports that, in November, homebuilders had a bleak view of current sales conditions, future sales expectations for the next six months and prospective buyer traffic.

“Persistent housing affordability challenges, including elevated home prices and mortgage rates, continue to weigh on prospective buyers and constrain demand,” Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, NAHB Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis, wrote in a note following today’s upcoming home sales release. “Builders are using sales incentives and price adjustments to attract buyers, but affordability remains a significant obstacle to a sustained recovery in housing demand.”.

A review of the latest earnings calls from 14 publicly traded homebuilders reveals that the country’s largest builders faced a challenging third quarter, with sales conditions remaining weak heading into the final months of the year, consistent with NAHB’s data.

Last quarter, only three of the public homebuilders — Smith Douglas Homes, Toll Brothers and Green Brick Partners — reported year-over-year increases in upcoming orders. However, nearly all 14 experienced sequential declines in orders, many exceeding 20%, pointing to a further deterioration in demand.

Sales volume followed a similar trend. Only Smith Douglas Homes and LGI Homes reported year-over-year increases in homes sold,.

Meanwhile, just two builders, Toll Brothers (2.4%) and Hovnanian Enterprises (0.4%), posted year-over-year increases in average sales prices. Toll’s luxury-focused buyer base is generally less sensitive to mortgage rates and economic volatility, while Hovnanian has increasingly shifted its product mix toward move-up and active-adult buyers, who tend to be more resilient to broader market pressures.

Many public homebuilders reported in October and November that buyers remain very cautious, which helped dampen sales volume and prices.

“As we moved through the quarter, our buyers became more cautious, did not feel an urgency to transact and felt more comfortable moving to the sidelines,” Century Communities Executive Chairman Dale Francescon said during an earnings call on October 28.

Paul Romanowski, President and CEO at D.R. Horton, acknowledged that October was another challenging month.

Sources indicate that “Demand did get weaker as the quarter went on, for sure. As rates rose and as we got into October, what we’ve seen mirrors September. Traffic and sales activity are somewhat below what we’d anticipate in a typical seasonal pattern,” he said during an earnings call on October 29.

Against this backdrop, it remains unclear whether October’s sales rebound reflects a meaningful improvement in demand or a temporary spike that could show up next month as a downward revision.

In a recent development, “Looking ahead, the question is whether enough buyers will follow those who signed contracts in October,” Kushi remarked, pointing to falling mortgage applications for new homes and low homebuilder confidence. “Builders are finding ways to make the monthly payment work for some buyers, but softer buyer traffic and fewer mortgage applications point to a tough winter.”.

#134509. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Fully Connected event

Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Fully Connected event

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.
  • Industry observers note that as inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs.
  • Recent findings suggest that “What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante remarked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:56 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.

Industry observers note that as inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs. The emergence of continuously learning agents and physical AI applications is further complicating that equation. For CoreWeave Inc., the changing workload mix is altering the economics of infrastructure delivery, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier.

Recent findings suggest that “What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante remarked. “They’ve got networking; they’ve got storage. They’ve got this software layer, which is observability. They’ve got security in there. They’ve got this closed-loop system between evaluation, observation [and] runtime curating … that’s sort of how they’re saying their software layer is now intact.”.

Sources indicate that during the Fully Connected event, Vellante and Furrier spoke with CoreWeave executives, technology partners and customers about the technical and economic realities of running artificial intelligence at production scale. (* Disclosure below.).

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video analysis with Dave Vellante and John Furrier:.

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s exclusive coverage of this event:.

Recent findings suggest that the commercial value of inference depends on both token volume and delivery speed. Nvidia Corp.’s Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator, which works with its Vera Rubin platform, is attracting interest in financial technology and other sectors that require real-time processing, according to Ian Buck, vice president and general manager of hyperscale and HPC at Nvidia.

“Data centers have a natural cap, and that cap is actually their power,” he told theCUBE. “With every generation of GPU, we make sure that our tokens per watt is upwards of 10 times more efficient. In fact, we saw that with Blackwell — we got, in the end, a 30x improvement in tokens per watt.”.

Memory management adds another dimension to AI infrastructure economics as agents engage in increasingly lengthy interactions. A single session involving 500,000 tokens can consume between 5% and 10% of a graphics processing unit’s memory. Retaining session context in persistent storage can reduce costly recalculations, according to Alon Horev, co-founder and chief technology officer of Vast Data Inc.

“You can move a session from one busy GPU to one less busy GPU and move KV cache either over the network or read it from Vast,” he told theCUBE. “Once you look at inference as a distributed problem where you have the opportunity to use GPU memory, CPU memory and Vast across a fleet of machines, you have more optionality and you have more optimized scheduling.”.

In a recent development, for AI-native startups, specialized cloud providers offer an alternative to owning capital-intensive infrastructure. LlamaIndex Inc. processes millions of document pages daily for customers in finance, legal services and insurance. Inference accounts for about 75% of its workloads, with training accounting for the remainder, according to Jerry Liu, co-founder and chief executive officer of LlamaIndex.

Industry observers note that “We serve a lot of different customers at extremely persistent and also spiky workloads,” he told theCUBE. “We really, really need to make sure that we have the right capacity to serve our customers without getting throttled.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Ian Buck:.

In a recent development, protecting AI infrastructure investments starts on the factory floor. Dell Technologies Inc. has developed modular rack designs to accommodate different power and cooling configurations. Its collaboration with CoreWeave includes integrating the cloud provider’s Racky management software into factory testing and improving liquid-cooling leak detection, according to Sarat Krishnan, director of PowerEdge AI architecture and systems development engineering at Dell.

Recent findings suggest that “It becomes increasingly expensive to remediate and fix something as you go later on in the manufacturing process; [it] becomes extremely expensive if you have to replace something in the data center,” he told theCUBE. “What we have done over the last two years is shift our most complex diagnostics — the ones that are going to capture true hardware failures — further and further left.”.

At Cognition AI Inc., continuous model improvement involves training across data centers in multiple countries. The company’s Devin software engineering agent now handles tasks ranging from code development to resolving production issues, according to Chen Goldberg (pictured, left), executive vice president of product and engineering at CoreWeave, and Silas Alberti (right), head of research and founding team at Cognition. To support these learning systems, CoreWeave introduced Forge, a platform that connects inference, evaluation and model refinement and incorporates Agent Lens to trace agent activity.

In a recent development, “If you run a big training run, you’re not just looking at the GPUs, but you also want uptime,” Alberti said during the event. “If just one replica goes down, the whole training run goes down. I think a very important metric is getting to this 99.99% reliability.”.

Recent findings suggest that for International Business Machines Corp., the power and cooling demands of newer hardware helped drive its decision to work with CoreWeave. The relationship has since expanded to include joint engineering around identity management and workload isolation through CoreWeave Sandboxes. IBM also benchmarks the performance impact of security controls to inform architectural decisions, according to Brian Belgodere, senior technical staff member at IBM.

“This is a supply chain problem, top to bottom,” Belgodere told theCUBE. “It’s not just the hardware: it’s the firmware, kernel levels, code, your data provenance. Then you get into the whole world of agents, your images. It is an absolute provenance problem.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Brian Belgodere:.

Industry observers note that for organizations deploying physical AI, implementation time is a key consideration in AI infrastructure economics. Aston Martin F1, whose race cars generate a million data points per second each, operates under strict budget constraints and development deadlines. CoreWeave’s forward-deployed engineering approach brings specialized expertise to those operations, according to Richard Ahlfeld, senior vice president of physical AI at CoreWeave, and Eric Ernst, commercial technology ambassador of AMR GP Ltd., trading as Aston Martin F1.

It has been revealed that “We really need people that can be outside of the car development phase and come in with the fresh knowledge of what’s happening in this industry that is moving extremely quickly,” Ernst said during the event. “You can build as many processes as you want, call it agile, whatever you want. You cannot stop that process. You got to hit a deadline.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Richard Ahlfeld and Eric Ernst:.

Walden Robotics Inc. uses large-scale virtual simulation to prepare robots for physical deployment. Its robots have been working full production shifts alongside humans since May, performing tasks such as machine tending, parts kitting and subassembly, according to Adrien Gaidon, co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics, and John Mancuso, vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc.

Industry observers note that “If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon told theCUBE. “We do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s full video discussion with John Mancuso and Adrien Gaidon:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blockstream CEO Adam Back has explained the overnight sell-off on Kraken's Canadian-dollar markets that sent the exchange's BTC/CAD pair to C$24,250, or roughly $17,000, on Saturday morning, and said that the drop started with the exchange's local USD/CAD market maker.

The Blockstream CEO addressed the problem on X on Saturday in a reply to a post that tracked large sell orders hitting Kraken's BTC/CAD order book at regular intervals throughout the night.

Industry observers note that the $17,000 figure is based on the Bank of Canada's Friday rate of C$1.4325 per U.S. dollar. Kraken's BTC/CAD pair printed the C$24,250 low on Saturday morning, according to TradingView data.

"No, the reason was USDCAD Kraken local spot FX market-maker ran out of money, as it has depegged away from market rate 1.434," Back replied.

In the same post, the Blockstream CEO said that it was "more accurate to say you could buy CAD discounted.".

It has been revealed that later, another X user argued that the Canadian dollar was in fact overvalued on Kraken during the sell-off, since anyone who held CAD could buy anything at a discount. Back agreed with the correction.

In a recent development, "You are right. BTCUSD normal price, USDCAD CAD mispriced, like a shortage of CAD bid the price up," Back wrote.

On Sunday, the Blockstream CEO described the whole chain of events in two more posts on X.

According to recent reports, according to Back, if the USD/CAD market maker failed, there were few buyers of BTC in Canadian dollars, and so the BTC/CAD price fell. In his view, traders would normally close such a gap with an arbitrage trade "by selling USD to CAD to buy if it BTCCAD doesn't track BTCUSD.".

Back wrote that the drop "liquidated people" and triggered stop losses "based on a local false price.".

"And then USDCAD followed because you could buy BTC cheaply in CAD, so it became logical to buy CAD way over par to take that arb," he added.

The BTC/CAD pair recovered later on Saturday, and on Sunday, it traded at C$86,236 on Kraken, according to TradingView.

Kraken said in a statement that its Canadian-dollar trading pairs faced heavy selling pressure starting around 20:00 UTC on Friday, and prices on these pairs fell significantly below those on other markets.

The Kraken sell-off started on the same day that Bitcoin dropped to $59,370, its lowest level since July 2, according to CoinGlass data. On Friday, CoinGlass also recorded $1.57 billion in liquidations across the crypto market over 24 hours, and long positions accounted for $1.43 billion of that amount.

Still, the exchange stated that every order was processed correctly and that its security teams found no evidence of a breach or compromised accounts.

"Executed trades stand," Kraken said.

Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.
  • Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.
  • The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest revision on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

According to recent reports, on Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp stated Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the firm looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

In a recent development, the finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn debuts reserved for Leo.

Recent findings suggest that ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA remarked.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

Latest Update: Court upholds NYC rent freeze backed by Mayor Mamdani

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (497 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Thanksgiving eve, Judge Brendan Lantry dismissed a landlords’ challenge to the Rent Guidelines Board’s late June decision to freeze rents.
  • With the national real estate industry watching, the rent freeze became a major test of what a mayor can do to force affordability.
  • Owners of rent-stabilized buildings argued that Mamdani stacked the board with loyalists after promising a freeze, making the outcome predetermined.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Thanksgiving eve, Judge Brendan Lantry dismissed a landlords’ challenge to the Rent Guidelines Board’s late June decision to freeze rents. The ruling upholds the city’s first-ever freeze on both one- and two-year leases.

With the national real estate industry watching, the rent freeze became a major test of what a mayor can do to force affordability.

Owners of rent-stabilized buildings argued that Mamdani stacked the board with loyalists after promising a freeze, making the outcome predetermined. They also accused the board of following a campaign promise instead of the data on rising landlord costs. Lantry rejected both claims.

The ruling comes three weeks after an appeals court revived the city’s pied-à-terre tax rollout on second homes valued at $5 million or higher. Mamdani posted on social media that the city has billed owners of those homes more than $500 million.

In a recent development, that lawsuit ran parallel to the rent freeze lawsuit landlords filed in late July. It originally was in a Staten Island court but was moved to Manhattan in August at the city’s request.

Recent findings suggest that the rent freeze took effect Oct. 1 while the lawsuit was pending and covers leases on more than a million apartments. The board had frozen one-year leases in 2015, 2016 and 2020.

According to recent reports, because the board acts in a quasi-legislative role, its orders stand if they have a rational basis, and courts may not substitute their own judgment, Lantry wrote. He found that the board’s 42-page explanatory statement highlighted it considered each factor the Administrative Code requires, including the industry’s economic condition and the cost of living.

Lantry said appointees who share the mayor’s views did not show collusion. He noted that “elections have consequences.”.

But Lantry did not let Mamdani completely off the hook.

In a recent development, “Regarding Mayor Mamdani’s campaign for Mayor of Upcoming York City, the court would be remiss not to state that such comments, promises, and guarantees to freeze the rent were reckless and irresponsible,” he wrote. “The Mayor of the City of New York has no authority to unilaterally raise, ‘freeze’ or otherwise adjust the rent of stabilized units in this City – that responsibility is within the power of the Board and the Board alone.”.

Industry observers note that he called an email in which the board’s chair shared a draft of the explanatory statement with a mayoral aide before the vote “troubling.” He remarked it cast a “dark shadow” over the board’s independence. Without more, he wrote, the email did not justify overturning the decision under Article 78, the state law that lets courts review government agency actions.

The judge noted that petitioners agreed to end court-ordered discovery, which produced about 1,000 documents, and never sought depositions.

According to recent reports, lantry acknowledged the freeze could make it harder for owners to refinance or renovate. But he wrote that the legal question is not whether the policy is wise.

Breaking: Three XRP Features Race for Last-Minute 2026 Activation: What Remains

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (434 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In the final stretch of 2026, some XRP Ledger protocol features await mainnet activation, with validator support and amendment voting as the final steps to bring upcoming functionality to the XRPL network.
  • In light of this, three amendments are racing against the 2026 calendar, with only a few votes left to reach a majority and enter the two-week activation period.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

In the final stretch of 2026, some XRP Ledger protocol features await mainnet activation, with validator support and amendment voting as the final steps to bring upcoming functionality to the XRPL network.

In light of this, three amendments are racing against the 2026 calendar, with only a few votes left to reach a majority and enter the two-week activation period. These include SingleAssetVault, LendingProtocol and confidential transfers.

All three remain below the required validator approval threshold of over 80% support, making the final weeks of the year increasingly crucial for their activation prospects.

With about five weeks left in 2026, activation remains possible this year, but additional validator support for each amendment must arrive soon enough and be sustained to complete the required two-week activation window.

In a recent development, the lending protocol allows on-chain fixed-term, uncollateralized loans from pooled funds in a Single Asset Vault. There are two amendments: LendingProtocolV1_1 and the original Lending Protocol amendment.

Industry observers note that the focus is on LendingProtocolV1_1, which extends the Lending Protocol and SingleAssetVault amendments with a upcoming closed-ended vault and cash-basis accounting. With the amendment, new loan brokers can only be created against closed-ended vaults.

In a recent development, lendingProtocolV1_1 has reached 70.59% support with 24 out of 34 validators voting yes, according to XRPScan data. It needs 28 votes to reach a majority, or more than 80% of 34 votes, meaning it has just four votes left.

A major privacy amendment for the XRP Ledger, confidential transfers, has 64.71% support and 22 of 34 validators voting yes. Confidential transfers, which rely on advanced cryptography (EC-ElGamal and ZKPs), offer institutional-grade privacy for Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs) and need six more yes votes to enter the activation window.

Recent findings suggest that singleAssetVault creates a structure for aggregating assets from multiple depositors and is intended to be used with the on-chain Lending Protocol. It has gained 73.53% support so far with 25 out of 34 validators voting in favor. Reaching more than 80% of 34 votes requires 28 votes; thus, three votes remain for it to enter the activation window.

#134503. Tech Report: Tesla confirms €3B Cybercab factory at Giga Berlin for up to 1M a year

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1310 w)
📖 Baca

Tech Report: Tesla confirms €3B Cybercab factory at Giga Berlin for up to 1M a year

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1310 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany.
  • According to recent reports, that’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one.
  • Plant manager André Thierig unveiled the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany. The company confirmed today a first €3 billion investment in a latest production building at Giga Berlin designed for up to 1 million Cybercabs a year, with production planned for 2029.

According to recent reports, that’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one. Under current EU rules, a driverless vehicle model is capped at 1,500 registrations a year.

Plant manager André Thierig unveiled the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.

It has been revealed that if you ever wondered, what we would be doing at Giga Berlin with all the land that we have… We are expanding! Cybercab production is coming to Giga Berlin! Today we confirmed a first investment of around € 3b in a fresh manufacturing building with an anticpated start of… pic.twitter.com/vpcDdxoqlW.

Per Tesla’s statement, the €3 billion pays for the upcoming production hall north of the existing plant, plus ancillary buildings and a second wastewater treatment plant. Tesla prepares to file the building application before the end of the year, break ground in the first half of 2027, and start production in 2029. The company says it will be “the technologically most advanced Tesla factory in the world.”.

Sources indicate that it leaked a few hours earlier. Steven Scholtysek, an automation engineer at the plant, posted that Elon Musk personally signed off on the project last week and that the new hall will be bigger than the original factory.

The building isn’t latest. Tesla laid out a blueprint to take Giga Berlin to 1 million vehicles a year in its 2023 permit filings and has been clearing land for it since. What’s new is the product. Until today, Tesla had only noted the second hall wouldn’t be another Model Y factory.

Giga Berlin still builds only the Model Y. Tesla has been hiring again at Giga Berlin this year as European demand came back, with a goal of 7,500 cars a week. Even at that pace, the plant would fall short of the 500,000 units a year Tesla promised when it opened in 2022.

Tesla is also adding 4680 battery cell production at the site, with 18 GWh of annual capacity planned.

So the newly introduced hall alone is rated for twice what the entire existing plant was supposed to build. And it comes after Musk tied the Berlin expansion to the plant’s works council election in March, warning workers against IG Metall’s influence.

Sources indicate that the EU has a type-approval path for fully driverless vehicles, but it’s a “small series” scheme limited to 1,500 registrations per vehicle type per year across the whole EU. In March, the Commission lifted that cap for automated valet parking. Robotaxis are still stuck in the small-series track.

Tesla also has no approval anywhere in Europe for its software to drive without supervision. The Dutch RDW approved the supervised version, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, and nine other countries recognize that approval. It still requires a driver paying attention. The Cybercab has no steering wheel.

Rules can move in three years. The Commission has remarked it wants large-series approval for other driverless uses, and a UN regulation for automated driving systems is in the works. But as of today, Tesla is committing €3 billion to a vehicle it can’t sell in volume in Europe.

According to recent reports, tesla could export from Berlin, of course. But 1 million Cybercabs a year on top of Giga Texas implies a robotaxi business many times bigger than anything on the road today. Texas, where Cybercab production started in April, had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October. And Tesla just opened personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly subscription, usable only inside its Robotaxi geofences.

According to recent reports, tesla can’t even launch its driver-assist system in Europe under its own name. What it’s rolling out there isn’t “Full Self-Driving.” It’s “Tesla Assisted Driving,” a level 2 system that needs a driver watching the road at all times, and it took a long fight with regulators to get it approved in 10 countries.

Industry observers note that the Cybercab is a much harder sell. No steering wheel, no pedals, so it has to be certified as a level 4 vehicle with nobody inside to take over. That’s a completely different approval from anything Tesla has gotten in Europe. As of this spring, the EU mentioned no automaker had even used its existing driverless approval path.

And the US program doesn’t inspire confidence. Robotaxi is still confined to geofences, still off highways, and it keeps crashing: Tesla had reported 22 incidents to NHTSA by July, and our analysis of the data earlier this year put it at one crash every 57,000 miles, roughly 9 times worse than the average human driver, with a safety monitor on board. The only reason those crashes don’t get more attention is that they happen at low speed. Of course they do. Tesla keeps the cars on slow city streets. Put the same system on the autobahn and we’d expect more crashes, and worse ones.

That’s the kind of news you have to want to believe. Tesla’s driver-assistance efforts are actually running into serious trouble in Europe. They still haven’t received approval for Level 2++ in Germany, while Mercedes, for example, already has it. They’ve also been told they can no longer use the term FSD because it’s considered misleading advertising. More importantly, Tesla isn’t conducting any Level 4 testing here, and that’s going to be a prerequisite for getting approvals in Europe. You can’t just self-certify your system in this field over here. So this is pretty typical Tesla news. A lot of hype, but absolutely nothing behind it.

Industry observers note that this is Musk’s modus operandi for the last few years: bet on autonomy before it’s ready. Tesla removed the Cybercab’s steering wheel assuming the software would be solved by the time it mattered. It wasn’t, and now Tesla is putting €3 billion into a German factory on the same assumption.

It has been revealed that good for the workers in Grünheide, and maybe the hall can build something else if this doesn’t work out. But spending €3 billion to build up to 1 million steering-wheel-less cars a year for a market where Tesla can’t legally run a single one, based on a program that hasn’t left the geofence in Texas, is extremely risky.

Sources indicate that will there be one unsupervised Cybercab carrying paying passengers in Europe when the Grünheide line starts in 2029? We wouldn’t bet on it.

Latest Update: AI infrastructure stocks continue their slide, but Anthropic closes higher

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Investors continued to offload artificial intelligence infrastructure stocks today, but Anthropic PBC recouped some of its losses from earlier this week.
  • In a recent development, the AI selloff reportedly began in August.
  • Industry observers note that nvidia closed at $173.73 the day before Huang’s resignation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:15 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Investors continued to offload artificial intelligence infrastructure stocks today, but Anthropic PBC recouped some of its losses from earlier this week.

In a recent development, the AI selloff reportedly began in August. It accelerated on Nov. 17, the day Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang resigned over his affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a cloud provider under investigation over alleged export control violations. Huang returned to the helm of the chipmaker Monday.

Industry observers note that nvidia closed at $173.73 the day before Huang’s resignation. It dropped as low as $125 during the executive’s two-week hiatus and surged 30% on Monday, the day he returned. Nvidia lost some of its recent gains in today’s trading session: Its share price closed 3.8% lower.

Industry observers note that other AI chip stocks have also taken a hit. Broadcom Inc. closed a small fraction of a percent lower than yesterday, while Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. fell 1.6% and 0.6%, respectively.

According to recent reports, the semiconductor stock that logged the biggest drop today is Ambarella Inc., a relatively low-profile maker of AI image analysis chips. Its accelerators are used by edge devices to process footage from their cameras. Ambarella dropped 19.8% today after closing 19% lower yesterday.

The stock’s decline was driven not so much by the broader AI selloff, but rather the weak earnings that Ambarella posted on Tuesday. The organization missed expectations across the board. Ambarella noted that some customers had canceled or delayed orders to mitigate the financial impact of soaring memory prices.

Sources indicate that micron Inc., one of the world’s top memory chip suppliers, saw its market capitalization drop more than 4.5% today. That’s despite CEO Sanjay Mehrotra’s recent disclosure that the manufacturer has already sold out 75% of its 2027 manufacturing capacity. According to the executive, the gap between memory demand and supply is only set to increase next year.

Companies downstream from chipmakers in the AI data center supply chain fared better. Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. ended the trading session 1.8% higher after dipping into the red earlier today, while Dell Technologies Inc. gained 0.64%.

In contrast, the major cloud providers weren’t left out of today’s selloff. Amazon.com Inc., the cloud market’s largest player, closed 3% lower. Microsoft Corp. and Google LLC dropped 1.25% and 2%, respectively. Oracle Corp., which trails the three companies in market share but has emerged as an vital AI infrastructure provider, took the biggest hit: It’s down 5% from yesterday.

It has been revealed that anthropic ended the trading session with a 1% gain. The organization thereby recouped some of yesterday’s losses, which pushed its stock below its $80 debut price. Anthropic went public last week through a record-setting offering that raised more than $93 billion.

Overall, the tech-heavy Nasdaq lost 0.6% while the S&P 500 slid 0.25%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 0.33%.
